title: The reliability of Deep Brain Stimulation YouTube videos
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study (§1 exclusion ground, §3 quality-vs-content rule). The only outcome is the DISCERN score, a 16-item instrument that grades whether a video states its aims, discloses its sources, and describes the risks, benefits and alternatives of treatment options. No item in the study judges any claim for truth or falsity against an external ground truth: there is no fact-check, no expert verification of factual accuracy, no guideline-concordance coding, and no explicit false/misleading label. A wholly accurate DBS video that simply fails to cite its sources or omits alternatives scores below 3 and is counted as 'poor', which is exactly the §3 test for QUALITY rather than CONTENT ('If a wholly true item could receive the label, it is QUALITY'). The abstract's language about 'accuracy' is not backed by any accuracy measurement. The paper's headline share is also a share of GOOD videos (24% scoring above 3), i.e. a positive-quality share rather than a misinformation share. Screened out under §1 because quality is the ONLY thing measured; see missed_or_uncertain for the fully coded QUALITY row an adjudicator can reinstate if the review chooses to carry quality-only papers as appendix QUALITY rows.
missed_or_uncertain:
ADJUDICATOR NOTE - §1 vs §3 tension. §1 lists 'QUALITY-ONLY studies (see §3)' as an exclusion ground, while §3 says a DISCERN score gives 'construct QUALITY (row kept, excluded from prevalence)'. I resolved this by treating §1 as governing the screen decision (this paper measures nothing but quality) and §3 as governing construct assignment within an otherwise eligible paper. If the review instead carries quality-only papers as appendix QUALITY rows, the row is fully specified here and can be reinstated verbatim: construct=QUALITY; country='United States' (searches run in the USA; the authors note results would differ elsewhere), country_scope=single; platform='YouTube', platform_norm=YouTube; date='May 2019', year='2019'; measure_type='% of DBS YouTube videos uploaded by universities or hospitals that scored above 3 on DISCERN (a "good" video)'; value_pct='24'; value_raw='only 10 (24%) scored greater than 3 (good score)' [Table 1 gives 'Rated as helpful 10*(0.24)'; Table 2 gives Number 10 for DISCERN>3 and 32 for DISCERN<=3]; value_kind=proportion; denominator='42 English-language DBS videos uploaded by universities, tertiary care centres or hospitals, drawn from the first three pages of YouTube relevance-ranked results for five keywords'; definition='video graded above 3 on the DISCERN instrument by one of four healthcare-personnel raters'; n='42 videos'; page_loc='Results p.2 and Discussion p.3; Tables 1 and 2'; population_scope=professional (all videos are institutional uploads); breadth='' (quality instrument, no veracity band); classification_level=claim_level; ground_truth=researcher_coding; ground_truth_detail='Four healthcare-personnel authors independently applied the validated DISCERN tool; 10 of 42 videos (24%) were graded by all four raters, giving 80% inter-rater agreement with a maximum 2-point spread, and the remaining 32 (76%) were split among graders'; unit=item; denom_scope=health_other topic with denom_selection=curated (first three pages of relevance-ranked results is a rank-truncated set); sampling_frame=curated_seed; topic=health_other; within_misinfo_content=false; borderline=true; confidence=high for the value, low for its relevance to prevalence.

Also available and NOT extracted: (a) the inverse share, 32/42 = 76.2% of videos scoring 3 or below (moderate/poor) - this IS permissible under R8 because Table 2 states both counts verbatim ('Number 10 | 32') against the same 42-video denominator, so it is an exact part/whole rather than a forbidden complement; it remains a QUALITY figure, not a misinformation prevalence, and I flag it only so an adjudicator sees the arithmetic is legitimate if the review wants the negative-side value. (b) Per-keyword good-video shares in Table 1: 'Deep Brain Stimulation' 9/28 (32%), 'DBS for Parkinson's Disease' 8/27 (30%), 'DBS for Essential Tremor' 5/24 (21%), 'DBS for Movement Disorders' 6/21 (29%) - these are overlapping keyword sets (the same video appears under several searches, which is why the assessed counts sum to 100 but the deduplicated total is 42), so they cannot be treated as independent estimates. (c) Engagement comparisons (duration 25.6 vs 3.0 min, P=0.01; views 56,126 vs 14,682; likes, dislikes, views/day) - these are correlates of quality, not prevalence or exposure, and the view counts have no misinformation numerator so no EXPOSURE or REACH row is derivable. No RECALL, CONTENT, SHARING or CONCENTRATION measure exists anywhere in the paper.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content appraisal of YouTube videos. Search run in May 2019 from the United States using five keywords ('Deep Brain Stimulation', 'DBS', 'DBS for Parkinson's disease', 'DBS for essential tremor', 'DBS for movement disorders'), taking the first three pages of results under YouTube's relevance-based ranking - a rank-truncated, algorithm-dependent and geographically dependent sample that the authors acknowledge would differ in other countries. Inclusion was restricted to English-language videos uploaded by a university, tertiary care centre or hospital, and duplicates and non-relevant videos were removed; the 'DBS' keyword yielded only one eligible video and was dropped. Final n=42 videos, which the authors themselves flag as a small sample, and which by construction excludes patient and private-practice uploads. Outcome: the DISCERN instrument (16 questions; 8 on reliability of information, 7 on treatment options, 1 overall quality rating), applied independently by four healthcare-personnel authors; >3 = 'good', =3 = 'moderate', <3 = 'poor'. Reliability: only 10 of 42 videos (24%) were graded by all four raters, yielding 80% agreement with a maximum 2-point scoring difference; the other 32 were split among graders with no double coding, so most of the sample has no reliability check. No formal kappa is reported. Analysis by Wilcoxon rank sum in R 3.6.0. IRB exempt (public data). No response rate applies. Critically for this review, the instrument measures information quality, not veracity, so no misinformation prevalence can be recovered from it.
rob.item6_quote: Videos with DISCERN greater than 3 are considered ‘‘good” videos. Videos with a grade equal to 3 are considered ‘‘moderate”. Videos with a score less than 3 are considered ‘‘poor”. According to the DISCERN Tool user guide, a threshold of 3 signifies that although videos are of moderate quality, they should be combined with additional sources for comprehensive understanding.
rob.item10_quote: Of the 42 videos included, only 10 (24%) scored greater than 3 (good score) (Tables 1 and 2).
